## Definition

Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Fix the compact noncommutative finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$, its Lie algebra $\mathfrak g=T_eG$, and a specified smooth finite-dimensional complex unitary representation $\rho:G\to U(W,h)$ on a Hermitian vector space $(W,h)$ supplied by a non-Abelian gauge datum. Thus the group multiplication and inversion are smooth, $G$ is compact in its manifold topology, and $\rho(g)$ preserves $h$ for every $g\in G$. No connection, principal bundle sector, action functional, or continuum theory is part of the lattice data below.

A **finite oriented lattice two-complex** is a finite set $\mathcal V$ of vertices, a finite set $\mathcal E^+$ containing one chosen orientation of each edge, an endpoint map $s,t:\mathcal E^+\to\mathcal V$, and a finite set $\mathcal F$ of faces. Each face $p\in\mathcal F$ is supplied with a based closed edge word $(e_1,\ldots,e_k)$ in the oriented edges $\mathcal E^+\sqcup\overline{\mathcal E^+}$, where the endpoint of each edge is the starting point of the next and the last endpoint is the first starting point. For the reverse orientation $\bar e$ of $e\in\mathcal E^+$, set $s(\bar e)=t(e)$ and $t(\bar e)=s(e)$.

A **link configuration** is a tuple $U=(U_e)_{e\in\mathcal E^+}\in G^{\mathcal E^+}$, with $U_{\bar e}:=U_e^{-1}$. The **holonomy of a face** $p=(e_1,\ldots,e_k)$ is the ordered product $U_p:=U_{e_1}\cdots U_{e_k}$ in traversal order, with the first traversed edge on the left. The vertex gauge group is $G^{\mathcal V}$ with coordinatewise multiplication; write $\mathbf e=(e)_{v\in\mathcal V}$ for its identity tuple. It acts by

$$
(h\cdot U)_e=h_{s(e)}U_eh_{t(e)}^{-1},\qquad h=(h_v)_{v\in\mathcal V}\in G^{\mathcal V}.
$$

Choose a normalized bi-invariant Borel probability measure $\mu_G$ on $G$. The link measure is the finite product $\mu_G^{\mathcal E^+}$. For each face choose a continuous function $\Phi_p:G\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $\Phi_p(gzg^{-1})=\Phi_p(z)$ and $\Phi_p(z^{-1})=\Phi_p(z)$. Define the dimensionless lattice action and its normalized expectation by

$$
S_\Lambda(U):=\sum_{p\in\mathcal F}\Phi_p(U_p),\qquad Z_\Lambda:=\int_{G^{\mathcal E^+}}e^{-S_\Lambda(U)}\,d\mu_G^{\mathcal E^+}(U),\qquad \langle O\rangle_\Lambda:=Z_\Lambda^{-1}\int_{G^{\mathcal E^+}}O(U)e^{-S_\Lambda(U)}\,d\mu_G^{\mathcal E^+}(U)
$$

for bounded measurable $O:G^{\mathcal E^+}\to\mathbb C$. The finite-volume **Gauss sector** is the closed subspace of $L^2(G^{\mathcal E^+},\mathbb P_\Lambda)$ consisting of measurable functions with finite integral of $|f|^2$, modulo equality $\mathbb P_\Lambda$-almost everywhere, whose equivalence classes are invariant under each element of $G^{\mathcal V}$. Here $\mathbb P_\Lambda$ is the normalized probability with density $Z_\Lambda^{-1}e^{-S_\Lambda}$ relative to product link measure. For $v\in\mathcal V$ and $X\in\mathfrak g$, let $X^{(v)}$ be the tangent vector at the identity of $G^{\mathcal V}$ with component $X$ at $v$ and zero at other vertices. If $\alpha(h,U)=h\cdot U$, define the infinitesimal **Gauss generator** on $C^\infty(G^{\mathcal E^+})$ by

$$
(D_{v,X}f)(U):=df_U\!\left(d\alpha_{(\mathbf e,U)}(X^{(v)},0)\right).
$$

The full Gauss sector uses invariance under every vertex gauge transformation; the infinitesimal equations $D_{v,X}f=0$ alone are not asserted to impose invariance under disconnected components of $G$. Link variables and the action are dimensionless. This finite mathematical regulator makes no continuum-limit or empirical claim.

## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every finite oriented lattice two-complex with compact Lie group $G$, normalized bi-invariant link probability $\mu_G$, and continuous conjugation-invariant face actions $\Phi_p$, the vertex formulas $(h\cdot U)_e=h_{s(e)}U_eh_{t(e)}^{-1}$ define a smooth group action on $G^{\mathcal E^+}$. Each face holonomy transforms by conjugation at its base vertex. Consequently the product Haar measure and the Boltzmann weight $e^{-\sum_p\Phi_p(U_p)}$ are gauge invariant, and the partition function satisfies $0<Z_\Lambda<\infty$. Thus the normalized finite-lattice expectation is a well-defined gauge-invariant probability expectation. In $L^2$ of that probability, the subspace of classes invariant under each vertex gauge transformation is closed. The infinitesimal Gauss generators defined by differentiating this smooth action are well-defined as directional derivatives on smooth functions.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a finite oriented two-complex, a compact Lie group $G$, a normalized bi-invariant probability $\mu_G$, and continuous class functions $\Phi_p$.

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is inherited through the supplied construction of $\mathfrak g=T_eG$; the definition does not use arbitrary choice. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] [[def-qftx-nonabelian-lattice-gauge-data]]: one variable $U_e\in G$ is assigned to each positively oriented edge, reverse edges carry $U_e^{-1}$, vertices act by $h_{s(e)}U_eh_{t(e)}^{-1}$, and face holonomies are ordered products around closed edge words.

[F2] [[def-qftx-nonabelian-lattice-gauge-data]]: $G$ is compact and $\mu_G$ is a normalized left- and right-invariant Borel probability; the face actions are continuous and conjugation invariant.

[F3] [[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]: the differential of a smooth map at a point sends tangent vectors at that point to tangent vectors at its image.

[F4] A finite product of sigma-finite measure spaces carries the unique product measure on the product sigma-algebra, with the rectangle formula; a finite product of probability measures is again a probability measure. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]] [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]

[F5] A nonnegative measurable density defines a measure by integration, and a normalized finite density defines a probability measure. [[def-measure-with-density]] [[def-probability-measure]] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]

[F6] The complex $L^2$ class uses $\|[f]\|_2=(\int |f|^2\,d\mathbb P_\Lambda)^{1/2}$ and the pairing $\langle[f],[g]\rangle=\int f\overline g\,d\mathbb P_\Lambda$; the cited result establishes representative-independence and norm properties. [[def-complex-l-two-inner-product]] [[thm-complex-l-two-inner-product-is-well-defined-and-cauchy-schwarz]]

[F7] The Lie group is second-countable, so its finite-product Borel sigma-algebra equals the product sigma-algebra; continuous face-holonomy, gauge-action, and density maps are measurable for these structures. [[def-lie-group]] [[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]] [[lem-borel-product-of-second-countable-spaces]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $h,k\in G^{\mathcal V}$, applying $k$ after $h$ sends an edge $e$ to $k_{s(e)}h_{s(e)}U_eh_{t(e)}^{-1}k_{t(e)}^{-1}=(kh)_{s(e)}U_e(kh)_{t(e)}^{-1}$; the identity tuple acts identically. Hence the formulas define a group action. Each coordinate is a composition of smooth multiplication and inversion maps, so the action map is smooth. By [F3], its differential sends the specified tangent vector at the identity of $G^{\mathcal V}$ to a tangent vector at $U$; applying $df_U$ therefore defines the stated directional derivative on every smooth $f$. The inherited axiom base is the stated $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ [A1]. [given, A1, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Around a face word based at $v_0$, the intermediate factors $h_{v_i}^{-1}h_{v_i}$ cancel, leaving $U_p(h\cdot U)=h_{v_0}U_p(U)h_{v_0}^{-1}$. Thus each $\Phi_p(U_p)$ and the total action are unchanged. For a fixed $h$, the inverse image of a measurable rectangle $\prod_e A_e$ under the link action is the rectangle $\prod_e(h_{s(e)}^{-1}A_eh_{t(e)})$; bi-invariance preserves each factor measure. The product-measure rectangle formula and uniqueness therefore show that the finite link product measure is gauge invariant on the full product sigma-algebra. [given, F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For each face $p$ and each $g\in G$, continuity of $\Phi_p$ gives an open neighborhood on which $|\Phi_p|\leq |\Phi_p(g)|+1$. Compactness of $G$ gives a finite subcover, so each $\Phi_p$ is bounded; summing over the finite face set gives $|S_\Lambda(U)|\leq M$ for some finite $M$. By [F7], the action, $S_\Lambda$, and its density are measurable; hence $e^{-M}\leq e^{-S_\Lambda(U)}\leq e^M$. Since the product link measure is a probability, $e^{-M}\leq Z_\Lambda\leq e^M$; in particular $0<Z_\Lambda<\infty$. The nonnegative density $Z_\Lambda^{-1}e^{-S_\Lambda}$ therefore defines the normalized probability measure $\mathbb P_\Lambda$. Its invariance follows from the invariance of the product measure and of $S_\Lambda$ in step 2.1. [given, F2, F4, F5, F7, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For each $h\in G^{\mathcal V}$, define $T_h[f]:=[U\mapsto f(h^{-1}\cdot U)]$ on complex $L^2(\mathbb P_\Lambda)$, with norm $\|[f]\|_2=(\int|f|^2\,d\mathbb P_\Lambda)^{1/2}$. Step 3.1 makes this well-defined and preserves the norm: invariance gives equality of integrals first for nonnegative simple functions and then, by the defining supremum for the nonnegative integral, for $|f|^2$. Thus each $T_h$ is a linear isometry. The invariant sector is exactly $\bigcap_{h\in G^{\mathcal V}}\ker(T_h-I)$; each $T_h-I$ is continuous by the norm triangle inequality, so its kernel is closed, and an arbitrary intersection of closed sets is closed. [F4, F6, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $G$ be a compact group with normalized bi-invariant Borel probability $\mu$. For positive integers $M,N$, let $\Lambda_{M,N}$ have vertices $(i,j)$ with $0\leq i\leq M$ and $0\leq j\leq N$, east-oriented horizontal edges $h_{i,j}:(i,j)\to(i+1,j)$ for $0\leq i<M$, $0\leq j\leq N$, north-oriented vertical edges $v_{i,j}:(i,j)\to(i,j+1)$ for $0\leq i\leq M$, $0\leq j<N$, and faces $p_{i,j}$ for $0\leq i<M$, $0\leq j<N$. The face $p_{i,j}$ has counterclockwise boundary word $(h_{i,j},v_{i+1,j},\bar h_{i,j+1},\bar v_{i,j})$, started at its lower-left vertex; multiply its link matrices in traversal order, with the first factor on the left. Let $G^{\mathcal V}$ act on positively oriented link variables by $(g\cdot U)_e=g_{s(e)}U_eg_{t(e)}^{-1}$. Use the product Haar measure $\mu^{\mathcal E^+}$ on links and free boundary edges. Give each face a positive continuous conjugation-invariant weight $w_{i,j}:G\to(0,\infty)$ with $w_{i,j}(g^{-1})=w_{i,j}(g)$, and normalize the density proportional to $\prod_{i,j}w_{i,j}(U_{p_{i,j}})$ relative to this link measure. For any chosen column $a\in\{0,\ldots,M\}$, fixing the gauge factor at $(a,0)$ to the identity gives a unique representative with every horizontal edge and every vertical edge in column $a$ equal to the identity. Write $V_{i,j}$ for the vertical link in this representative and set $P_{i,j}:=V_{i+1,j}V_{i,j}^{-1}$. The plaquette variables $(P_{i,j})$ are independent, and $P_{i,j}$ has probability

$$
d\nu_{i,j}(g)=\frac{w_{i,j}(g)}{\int_Gw_{i,j}(z)\,d\mu(z)}\,d\mu(g).
$$

This is a finite planar lattice statement with no periodic identifications or continuum limit.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a compact group $G$, a normalized bi-invariant probability $\mu$, the finite rectangular cellulation, and the stated positive class weights.

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is inherited through the supplied Lie-algebra construction in the finite lattice datum; the proof below uses only finite products and deterministic coordinate changes. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] [[def-qftx-nonabelian-lattice-gauge-data]]: edge variables are $G$-valued, reverse orientations carry inverses, vertices act by left and right multiplication at endpoints, and the link measure is a finite product of $\mu$.

[F2] [[def-qftx-nonabelian-lattice-gauge-data]]: each face holonomy is the ordered product around its oriented boundary, and the action weight is a continuous class function of that holonomy.

[F3] The finite lattice datum uses a compact finite-dimensional real Lie group; its underlying smooth manifold is Hausdorff and second-countable, and for finite products the Borel sigma-algebra equals the product of the factor Borel sigma-algebras. [[def-qftx-nonabelian-gauge-data]] [[def-lie-group]] [[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]] [[lem-borel-product-of-second-countable-spaces]]

[F4] A finite product of probability measures is a probability on the recursively defined product sigma-algebra; the product measure is characterized by its values on measurable rectangles. [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] [[def-probability-measure]] [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]] [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]

[F5] The integral is the Lebesgue integral on the stated measure space; a complex function is in $L^1$ when its absolute value has finite integral. A bounded measurable function on a probability space is in $L^1$ because $\int|f|\leq\|f\|_\infty$. [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]

[F6] Tonelli applies to nonnegative measurable functions on sigma-finite products, and Fubini applies to $L^1$ functions on sigma-finite products. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct change of variables.

1.1 Fix a column $a$. The set $T$ of all horizontal edges together with the vertical edges in column $a$ is a spanning tree: each row is a horizontal path and the selected vertical edges join these row paths in one vertical path, with no other vertical edge in $T$ to close a cycle. Thus $T$ connects every vertex and has no cycle. The only inherited set-theoretic premise is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ [A1]. [given, A1, F1, construct]

2.1 Fix the root $(a,0)$ and set its gauge factor to the identity. Recursively along $T$, each tree-edge condition $h_{s(e)}U_eh_{t(e)}^{-1}=1$ determines the as-yet-unknown gauge factor at the next vertex uniquely, using multiplication and inversion in $G$. Hence every link configuration has a unique root-fixed gauge transform whose tree links are the identity. [given, F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 First, inversion preserves $\mu$. For a bounded measurable $f$, the function $(x,y)\mapsto f(x^{-1}y)$ is product-measurable: by [F3], the product sigma-algebra is the Borel sigma-algebra of $G\times G$, and multiplication and inversion are continuous. Since $\mu\times\mu$ is a probability, its absolute integral is finite by [F5]. Set $I:=\int_G\int_G f(x^{-1}y)\,d\mu(y)\,d\mu(x)$. Fubini [F6] permits either order of integration. Integrating in $y$ first and using left invariance gives $I=\int_G f\,d\mu$. Reversing the order and, for fixed $y$, substituting $x=yx'$ (again left invariance) gives $I=\int_G f((x')^{-1})\,d\mu(x')$. Thus $\int f(x^{-1})d\mu(x)=\int f(x)d\mu(x)$, so inversion preserves $\mu$. With root factor $h_{(a,0)}=1$, the inverse coordinate map is $U_e=h_{s(e)}^{-1}h_{t(e)}$ on $T$ and $U_e=h_{s(e)}^{-1}V_eh_{t(e)}$ off $T$. Recovering each $h_v$ recursively along $T$ uses left or right translations and inversion; recovering each off-tree $U_e$ from fixed $h$ and $V_e$ uses left and right translations. These maps preserve each Haar factor, so successive finite Fubini integrations send $\prod_e d\mu(U_e)$ to $\prod_{v\ne(a,0)}d\mu(h_v)\prod_{e\notin T}d\mu(V_e)$; every bounded integrand used here is $L^1$ because all factors are probabilities. The tree coordinates integrate to $1$. [given, F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 For each face based at $v_0$, substituting the vertex action from [F1] into its ordered boundary product cancels every intermediate factor $h_{v_i}^{-1}h_{v_i}$ and gives $U_p(h\cdot U)=h_{v_0}U_p(U)h_{v_0}^{-1}$. Since each $w_{i,j}$ is conjugation-invariant by [F2], the full density $\prod_{i,j}w_{i,j}(U_{p_{i,j}})$ is unchanged by the gauge-fixing transformation. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 In tree gauge all horizontal variables are $1$ and $V_{a,j}=1$. The counterclockwise face word gives $P_{i,j}=V_{i+1,j}V_{i,j}^{-1}$. For a fixed row $j$, starting at $V_{a,j}=1$, the equations determine $V_{i+1,j}=P_{i,j}V_{i,j}$ to the right of $a$ and $V_{i,j}=P_{i,j}^{-1}V_{i+1,j}$ to its left. Thus the map from the $M$ non-tree vertical variables in row $j$ to its $M$ plaquette variables is a bijective triangular coordinate change. Recursively, to the right of $a$ the map from $P_{i,j}$ to $V_{i+1,j}$ is right translation by fixed $V_{i,j}$, while to the left it is inversion followed by right translation by fixed $V_{i+1,j}$; both preserve $\mu$ by bi-invariance and step 3.1. Iterated Fubini therefore shows that this row map preserves the product probability measure. Distinct rows use disjoint vertical variables, so their product gives a measure-preserving bijection from all non-tree vertical variables to all plaquette variables. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 By step 3.2 the gauge-fixed unnormalized density is $\prod_{i,j}w_{i,j}(P_{i,j})$. Each positive continuous $w_{i,j}$ is bounded above and below by positive constants: continuity gives a bounded neighborhood at each group element, and compactness gives a finite subcover; applying the same argument to $1/w_{i,j}$ gives a positive lower bound. Thus there are constants $0<m_{i,j}\leq w_{i,j}\leq M_{i,j}<\infty$, so the probability integral gives $0<m_{i,j}\leq z_{i,j}=\int_Gw_{i,j}\,d\mu\leq M_{i,j}<\infty$. In particular, each factor and the finite product density are $L^1$; Fubini [F6] applies to factor the partition function. The product Haar measure factors by step 4.1, so the partition function is $\prod_{i,j}z_{i,j}$; dividing by it yields the product of the displayed one-plaquette probability measures defined by the densities [F4]. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 3.2, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC and use the finite non-Abelian lattice-data interface with global group $SU(2)$ and its smooth defining unitary representation on standard $\mathbb C^2$. Let $N_s,N_t\geq3$ be finite integers and let $a>0$, $\beta>0$. Use the finite periodic Euclidean lattice $\Lambda=(\mathbb Z/N_s\mathbb Z)^3\times(\mathbb Z/N_t\mathbb Z)$, with its finite oriented two-complex of vertices, positive spatial edges $(x,i,t)$, temporal edges $(x,t)$, and oriented plaquette boundary words. On every positive edge put an independent matrix in the compact Hausdorff Lie group

$$SU(2)=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_2,\ \det U=1\},$$

and assign its inverse to reverse traversal. A vertex function $\Omega:\Lambda\to SU(2)$ acts on an oriented link $U_{vw}$ by $U_{vw}\mapsto\Omega_vU_{vw}\Omega_w^{-1}$. For each oriented plaquette $p$, let $U_p$ be the ordered product of its four boundary links, using inverse matrices for reverse traversals. Put

$$S_\Lambda(U)=\beta\sum_{p\in\mathcal P_\Lambda}\left(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2U_p\right).$$

Let $dU$ be the unique normalized left Haar Borel probability measure on $SU(2)$, which is also right invariant, and use it as the bi-invariant link measure in the finite lattice-data interface. Let $\mathcal C_\Lambda:=SU(2)^{\mathcal E^+}$ be the finite link-configuration space with the product Borel sigma-algebra $\bigotimes_{e\in\mathcal E^+}\mathcal B(SU(2))$, and let $d\mu_\Lambda$ be the finite product of $dU$ over all positive links, formed by the finite-product measure theorem. Define

$$Z_\Lambda=\int e^{-S_\Lambda(U)}\,d\mu_\Lambda(U).$$

For every bounded Borel-measurable function $O:\mathcal C_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$, the integral $\int Oe^{-S_\Lambda}\,d\mu_\Lambda$ is finite; moreover $0<Z_\Lambda\leq1$, so its normalized expectation is defined.

For a spatial slice $u=(U_{x,i})$, define the spatial plaquette action $S_s(u)$ by restricting the displayed action to spatial plaquettes. For two adjacent slices $u',u$ and temporal links $\eta_x$, define $S_t(u',u;\eta)$ by summing the same plaquette term over $\eta_xU'_{x,i}\eta_{x+\hat i}^{-1}U_{x,i}^{-1}$. Let $d\mu_s,d\mu_V$ be the corresponding finite product Haar probabilities, let $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}=L^2(SU(2)^{E_s},d\mu_s;\mathbb C)$, and for $h\in SU(2)^{V_s}$ set $(\mathcal U(h)\psi)(u)=\psi(h^{-1}\cdot u)$, with equality in $L^2$. Define $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}=\{\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm kin}:\mathcal U(h)\psi=\psi\text{ for every }h\in SU(2)^{V_s}\}$.

$$K(u',u)=e^{-\frac12S_s(u')-\frac12S_s(u)}\int e^{-S_t(u',u;\eta)}\,d\mu_V(\eta),\qquad (T\psi)(u')=\int K(u',u)\psi(u)\,d\mu_s(u).$$

Then $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ is closed and contains the nonzero constant function. $T$ is a bounded operator on $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$ with $\|T\|\leq1$ and maps $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$ into $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$. The cyclic product of $N_t$ kernels integrates to $Z_\Lambda$; insertion of any bounded slice observable gives the corresponding finite-volume unnormalized expectation. No self-adjointness, positivity as a quadratic form, Hamiltonian limit, or continuum statement is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC; finite $N_s,N_t\geq3$, $a,\beta>0$; the finite oriented lattice and compact-group link-data convention stated above.

[A1] Full AC, written as the choice-function axiom, is used for normalized Haar existence and implies Countable Choice: apply its choice function to the image set of any countable family of nonempty sets and compose with the family indexing map. This supplies the Countable Choice hypothesis of [F5]. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] [[cor-normalized-haar-probability-on-a-compact-group]]: under full AC, a compact Hausdorff group has a unique normalized left Haar probability, also right invariant.

[F2] [[lem-qftx-su2-compact-nonabelian-group]]: the displayed matrix group is a compact Hausdorff non-Abelian finite-dimensional real Lie group; its defining matrix representation is smooth and unitary, and $\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2V\in[-1,1]$.

[F3] [[def-qftx-nonabelian-lattice-gauge-data]]: the actual finite-lattice interface takes a finite oriented two-complex and a supplied compact noncommutative finite-dimensional Lie group with smooth unitary representation; it assigns group elements to positively oriented edges, uses inverses on reversed edges, defines the vertex gauge action and ordered face holonomies, chooses a normalized bi-invariant Borel probability and its finite product, and uses continuous conjugation- and inverse-invariant face potentials.

[F4] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] makes parameter integrals of nonnegative measurable product functions measurable and permits the iterated finite-lattice integrations.

[F5] [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]: under Countable Choice, for every measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ the quotient $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ of measurable square-integrable complex functions by almost-everywhere equality is a complex Hilbert space with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$, linear in the first variable, inducing the quotient norm $\|f\|_2^2=\int|f|^2\,d\mu$. No completeness or sigma-finiteness of the measure is required.

[F6] [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]: for sigma-finite factor measures, the product measure exists and has the rectangle formula. Applying this two-factor theorem successively to the finite list of Haar probability factors gives the finite product measure; at each stage its total mass is one by the rectangle formula.

[F7] [[thm-complex-l-two-inner-product-is-well-defined-and-cauchy-schwarz]]: on every measure space the displayed complex integral pairing is representative-independent and satisfies $|\langle f,g\rangle|\leq\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$. In particular this applies on the original finite-product Haar slice measure, without passing to its completion.

## Proof

1.1 For $V\in SU(2)$, the parametrization in [F2] gives $\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2V\in[-1,1]$ and a real trace. Thus $\Phi(V)=\beta(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2V)$ is continuous. Cyclicity of trace gives $\operatorname{Tr}_2(gVg^{-1})=\operatorname{Tr}_2V$; unitarity gives $\operatorname{Tr}_2(V^{-1})=\overline{\operatorname{Tr}_2V}=\operatorname{Tr}_2V$. Hence each plaquette potential is conjugation- and inverse-invariant as required by [F3]. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Each plaquette term therefore lies in $[0,2]$. Since $\mathcal P_\Lambda$ is finite, $0\leq S_\Lambda\leq2\beta|\mathcal P_\Lambda|$, and consequently $e^{-2\beta|\mathcal P_\Lambda|}\leq e^{-S_\Lambda}\leq1$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The actions $S_s,S_t$ are sums of nonnegative plaquette terms by step 1.1, so $0\leq K(u',u)\leq1$. Matrix multiplication, inversion on $SU(2)$, and trace are continuous, so the temporal-action integrand is nonnegative and product-measurable. The slice and vertex product Haar measures are probabilities by [F1,F6], hence sigma-finite; Tonelli [F4] makes the $\eta$-integral $K$ measurable in $(u',u)$. Each slice Haar product is a probability by [F6], so $\int|K|^2\,d(\mu_s\times\mu_s)\leq1$. [given, F1, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The compact Hausdorff group in [F2] has its normalized Haar probability by [F1]. Apply the two-factor product-measure theorem [F6] successively along the finite ordered link set; the rectangle formula at each stage gives total mass one, and [F3] identifies this iterated product with $d\mu_\Lambda$. Integrating the bounds in step 2.1 gives $e^{-2\beta|\mathcal P_\Lambda|}\leq Z_\Lambda\leq1$. For bounded $O$, $\left|\int Oe^{-S_\Lambda}\,d\mu_\Lambda\right|\leq\|O\|_\infty Z_\Lambda<\infty$; division by the positive lower bound for $Z_\Lambda$ defines its normalized expectation. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Apply [F5] to $X_s=SU(2)^{E_s}$ with $\mathcal A_s=\bigotimes_{e\in E_s}\mathcal B(SU(2))$ and its original product probability $\mu_s$ from [F6]; [A1] supplies Countable Choice, so $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$ is a complex Hilbert space with the pairing in [F5]. Let $\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$ and choose a measurable representative. Since $d\mu_s$ is a probability, [F7] applied to $|\psi|$ and the constant function $1$ of norm one gives $\|\psi\|_{L^1(d\mu_s)}\leq\|\psi\|_{L^2(d\mu_s)}$. The kernel $K$ is measurable and satisfies $0\leq K\leq1$ by step 2.2, so $\int K(u',u)\psi(u)\,d\mu_s(u)$ converges absolutely for every $u'$ and is independent of the representative of $\psi$. The product function $(u',u)\mapsto K(u',u)\psi(u)$ is measurable, and its absolute integral over $d\mu_s(u')d\mu_s(u)$ is at most $\|\psi\|_{L^1(d\mu_s)}$; Tonelli [F4] applied to the positive and negative parts of its real and imaginary parts shows that the section integral $T\psi$ is measurable. For each $u'$, both $K(u',\cdot)^{1/2}$ and $K(u',\cdot)^{1/2}\psi$ lie in $L^2(d\mu_s)$, so [F7] applied to $K(u',\cdot)^{1/2}\psi$ and $K(u',\cdot)^{1/2}$ gives $|T\psi(u')|^2\leq\big(\int K(u',u)\,d\mu_s(u)\big)\big(\int K(u',u)|\psi(u)|^2\,d\mu_s(u)\big)\leq\int K(u',u)|\psi(u)|^2\,d\mu_s(u)$, because the first factor is at most one. Integrating in $u'$ and applying Tonelli again yields $\|T\psi\|_{L^2(d\mu_s)}^2\leq\int |\psi(u)|^2\big(\int K(u',u)\,d\mu_s(u')\big)d\mu_s(u)\leq\|\psi\|_{L^2(d\mu_s)}^2$, since $K\leq1$ and $d\mu_s$ is a probability. Linearity follows from linearity of the absolutely convergent section integral. Thus $T$ is a well-defined bounded linear operator with $\|T\|\leq1$. [A1, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Each spatial-link transformation is a left and right translation, so it preserves its Haar factor by [F1]; the rectangle formula and uniqueness in [F6] then show the product slice measure $d\mu_s$ is preserved. Under independent gauge transformations $h,h'$ of the incoming and outgoing slices, change temporal-link variables by $\eta_x\mapsto h_x\eta_x(h'_x)^{-1}$. Each such coordinate map also preserves Haar factors by [F1], and thus preserves $d\mu_V$ by [F6]. Substitution in $Q_{x,i}=\eta_xU'_{x,i}\eta_{x+\hat i}^{-1}U_{x,i}^{-1}$ cancels the neighboring $h'$ matrices and gives $Q_{x,i}\mapsto h_xQ_{x,i}h_x^{-1}$; each spatial plaquette is likewise conjugated at its base vertex. Trace invariance therefore preserves $S_t,S_s$, and the temporal integration gives $K(h'\cdot u',h\cdot u)=K(u',u)$ for every pair $(h',h)$. In particular, setting $h=1$ gives $K(h'\cdot u',u)=K(u',u)$. The pointwise integral definition established in step 3.2 now implies $(T\psi)(h'\cdot u')=(T\psi)(u')$ for every $u'$, hence as $L^2$ classes for each fixed $h'$, so $T\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$. The constant function has norm one because $d\mu_s$ is a probability and is fixed by every gauge transformation, so it is a nonzero physical vector. [given, A1, F1, F3, F5, F6, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 Measure preservation from step 4.1 implies that pullback by $h^{-1}$ preserves measurable null sets, so $\mathcal U(h)$ is well-defined on almost-everywhere classes. It preserves the integral pairing from [F5] and has inverse $\mathcal U(h^{-1})$, hence is unitary on the complex Hilbert space established in step 3.2. Its fixed space is the kernel of the bounded operator $\mathcal U(h)-I$, hence is closed; the intersection over all $h$ is $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$, so $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ is closed. [given, A1, F5, step 3.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 In the cyclic product of kernels, each time slice contributes one half of $S_s(u_t)$ from the incoming factor and one half from the outgoing factor, summing to the full spatial action. Each temporal-link integral contributes exactly $e^{-S_t(u_{t+1},u_t;\eta_t)}$. Therefore the product integrand before temporal-link integration is the full $e^{-S_\Lambda}$; finite-product Tonelli [F4] gives the cyclic-kernel integral $Z_\Lambda$. For a bounded slice observable $O(u_0)$, the absolute value of its inserted integrand is bounded by $\|O\|_\infty e^{-S_\Lambda}\leq\|O\|_\infty$ on the finite product probability space [F6], so it is integrable. Applying [F4] to the positive and negative parts of its real and imaginary components justifies exchanging the integrations; the result is the corresponding unnormalized finite-volume expectation. [given, F3, F4, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Postulate

Adopt the following pure-gauge Euclidean regulator. Assume full AC for normalized Haar-probability existence and for the L² transfer-operator framework. Let $N_s,N_t\geq3$ be integers, $a>0$ a common lattice spacing, and $g_0>0$ a dimensionless bare coupling. Use natural units $\hbar=c=1$. The finite periodic lattice is

$$\Lambda=(\mathbb Z/N_s\mathbb Z)^3\times(\mathbb Z/N_t\mathbb Z),$$

with spatial extent $L_s=N_sa$ in each spatial direction and Euclidean time extent $L_t=N_ta$. The global gauge group supplied by the finite non-Abelian lattice datum is

$$SU(2)=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_2,\ \det U=1\},$$

the compact Hausdorff non-Abelian Lie group established in the preceding local lemma, with its smooth defining two-dimensional unitary representation. Use that representation; $U^*$ denotes conjugate transpose and $\operatorname{Tr}_2$ its matrix trace. All link variables are dimensionless.

For each positive spatial direction $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, assign a link matrix $U_{x,i,t}\in SU(2)$ from $(x,t)$ to $(x+\hat i,t)$. Assign a temporal link matrix $\eta_{x,t}\in SU(2)$ from $(x,t)$ to $(x,t+1)$, with time understood modulo $N_t$. A reversed link carries the inverse matrix. Vertex gauge transformations are all functions $\Omega:\Lambda\to SU(2)$, acting by

$$U_{x,i,t}\mapsto \Omega_{x,t}U_{x,i,t}\Omega_{x+\hat i,t}^{-1},\qquad \eta_{x,t}\mapsto\Omega_{x,t}\eta_{x,t}\Omega_{x,t+1}^{-1}.$$

Let $E_\Lambda^+$ be the finite set of these positively oriented spatial and temporal links, let $\mathcal C_\Lambda:=SU(2)^{E_\Lambda^+}$ be the full link-configuration space with its finite-product topology, and equip it with the product Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B_\Lambda:=\bigotimes_{\ell\in E_\Lambda^+}\mathcal B(SU(2))$.

For $i<j$, define the spatial plaquette product

$$U_{x,ij,t}=U_{x,i,t}U_{x+\hat i,j,t}U_{x+\hat j,i,t}^{-1}U_{x,j,t}^{-1},$$

and define the temporal-spatial plaquette product

$$Q_{x,i,t}=\eta_{x,t}U_{x,i,t+1}\eta_{x+\hat i,t}^{-1}U_{x,i,t}^{-1}.$$

Set $\beta=4/g_0^2$, a positive dimensionless parameter. For a spatial slice $u=(U_{x,i})$, set

$$S_s(u)=\beta\sum_{x,\ i<j}\left(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2 U_{x,ij}\right),$$

and for adjacent slices $u',u$ and temporal links $\eta=(\eta_x)$, set

$$S_t(u',u;\eta)=\beta\sum_{x,\ i}\left(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{ReTr}_2(\eta_xU'_{x,i}\eta_{x+\hat i}^{-1}U_{x,i}^{-1})\right).$$

The adopted Wilson action is $S_\Lambda=\sum_{t=0}^{N_t-1}\big(S_s(u_t)+S_t(u_{t+1},u_t;\eta_t)\big)$, with $u_{N_t}=u_0$. The compact Hausdorff group $SU(2)$ has the unique normalized left Haar probability measure $dU$, which is also right invariant under the assumed Axiom of Choice. On each positively oriented link use this measure; $d\mu_\Lambda$ is its finite product over the link set. For a bounded $\mathcal B_\Lambda$-measurable function $O:\mathcal C_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$, call $O$ gauge-invariant when $O(\Omega\cdot U)=O(U)$ for every vertex transformation $\Omega:\Lambda\to SU(2)$ and every $U\in\mathcal C_\Lambda$, where $\Omega\cdot U$ is the link configuration whose coordinates are the transformed links displayed above. The exact finite-volume partition function and the expectation of each such observable are

$$Z_\Lambda=\int e^{-S_\Lambda}\,d\mu_\Lambda,\qquad \langle O\rangle_\Lambda=Z_\Lambda^{-1}\int Oe^{-S_\Lambda}\,d\mu_\Lambda.$$

If $O$ represents a physical observable with assigned units, $\langle O\rangle_\Lambda$ has those same units; this postulate assigns no unit to the generic mathematical function $O$.

For the transfer convention, let $V_s=(\mathbb Z/N_s\mathbb Z)^3$ be the finite vertex set of one slice and $E_s=V_s\times\{1,2,3\}$ its positive spatial-link set. Define $d\mu_s:=\bigotimes_{(x,i)\in E_s}dU$ on $SU(2)^{E_s}$, where each factor is the normalized Haar Borel probability; let $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}=L^2(SU(2)^{E_s},d\mu_s;\mathbb C)$ be the complex $L^2$ space. Define $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}=\{\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm kin}:\mathcal U(h)\psi=\psi\text{ for every }h\in SU(2)^{V_s}\}$, where $\mathcal U(h)\psi(u)=\psi(h^{-1}\!\cdot u)$ in $L^2$. The finite-lattice well-definedness result establishes that this fixed subspace is closed. It is the group-invariant finite-slice Gauss sector. For one transfer step let $\eta=(\eta_x)_{x\in V_s}\in SU(2)^{V_s}$ denote its temporal-link tuple, and define $d\mu_V:=\bigotimes_{x\in V_s}dU$ on those coordinates, with each factor the normalized Haar Borel probability $dU$. Thus $d\mu_V$ is the finite product probability over all temporal links in one time step. Define

$$K(u',u)=e^{-\frac12S_s(u')-\frac12S_s(u)}\int_{SU(2)^{V_s}}e^{-S_t(u',u;\eta)}\,d\mu_V(\eta),\qquad (T\psi)(u')=\int K(u',u)\psi(u)\,d\mu_s(u).$$

The finite Euclidean time direction is assembled by iterating this one-step transfer operator, with the periodic boundary identification stated above. This is a Euclidean transfer convention only: no self-adjoint or positive-spectrum claim for $T$, no Lorentzian Hamiltonian identification, and no continuum or infinite-volume limit are postulated. The model has no dynamical matter fields, so it makes no matter-screening, confinement, or string-breaking claim. The regulator is adopted, not derived from a continuum theory or empirical evidence.

The quantities $a,L_s,L_t$ have units of length; $g_0,\beta,U_{x,i,t},\eta_{x,t},S_\Lambda,Z_\Lambda$ are dimensionless in the stated natural-unit convention. No measured parameter is supplied.

## Definition

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and take finite oriented lattice data with compact group $G$, link variables $U_e$, and vertex action $U_e\mapsto h_{s(e)}U_eh_{t(e)}^{-1}$. Fix a positive-dimensional finite-dimensional complex Hermitian space $(W,h)$ and a smooth group homomorphism $\rho:G\to U(W,h)$, where $U(W,h)$ is the group of invertible complex-linear maps preserving $h$; put $d=\dim_{\mathbb C}W\geq1$. A **based closed lattice loop** is a finite edge word $C=(e_1,\ldots,e_\ell)$ of integer length $\ell\geq0$ with a chosen base vertex $v_0$, such that consecutive endpoints match and, when $\ell>0$, the first and last endpoints are $v_0$; when $\ell=0$, the loop consists only of $v_0$. Its ordered holonomy is $U_C:=U_{e_1}\cdots U_{e_\ell}$, in traversal order with the first edge on the left; for $\ell=0$, set $U_C=e$. The reversed word is $C^{-1}=(\bar e_\ell,\ldots,\bar e_1)$. The **normalized Wilson loop** is

$$
W_\rho(C;U):=\frac{1}{d}\operatorname{Tr}_W\!\big(\rho(U_C)\big).
$$

The loop is dimensionless. Changing the base vertex by a cyclic rebase conjugates $U_C$ and leaves $W_\rho$ unchanged; reversing the loop gives $W_\rho(C^{-1};U)=\overline{W_\rho(C;U)}$. On a fixed finite lattice with a specified finite product Haar probability and bounded action, $\langle W_\rho(C)\rangle_\Lambda$ is the ordinary normalized finite-dimensional integral. No renormalized continuum Wilson loop or continuum limit is defined here.

## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $G$ be a group and let $(W,q)$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hermitian inner-product space. Define $U(W,q):=\{T\in\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbb C}(W):q(Tu,Tv)=q(u,v)\text{ for all }u,v\in W\}$, and let $\rho:G\to U(W,q)$ be a group homomorphism, with $d=\dim_{\mathbb C}W\geq1$. Let a finite oriented graph have vertices $\mathcal V$ and one chosen orientation $\mathcal E^+$ for each edge; for $e\in\mathcal E^+$ write $s(e),t(e)$ for its source and target. A link configuration assigns $U_e\in G$ to each $e\in\mathcal E^+$ and sets $U_{\bar e}=U_e^{-1}$. A based closed edge word $C=(e_1,\ldots,e_\ell)$ has length $\ell\geq0$, consecutive endpoints match, and when $\ell>0$ it starts and ends at a chosen vertex $v_0$; for $\ell=0$ it consists only of $v_0$. Put $U_C:=U_{e_1}\cdots U_{e_\ell}$ in traversal order, with the empty product equal to the identity, and put $W_\rho(C;U):=d^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}_W(\rho(U_C))$. For every vertex tuple $k\in G^{\mathcal V}$ acting by $(k\cdot U)_e=k_{s(e)}U_ek_{t(e)}^{-1}$, one has $U_C(k\cdot U)=k_{v_0}U_C(U)k_{v_0}^{-1}$. Thus the normalized trace is gauge invariant and unchanged when the based word is cyclically rotated; for $\ell>0$ reversal is $C^{-1}=(\bar e_\ell,\ldots,\bar e_1)$, while the empty word reverses to itself, and $W_\rho(C^{-1};U)=\overline{W_\rho(C;U)}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the finite link gauge action, a based closed edge word $C=(e_1,\ldots,e_\ell)$, and a finite-dimensional unitary representation $\rho$.

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is inherited through the finite non-Abelian lattice datum. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] [[def-qftx-nonabelian-lattice-gauge-data]]: $(h\cdot U)_e=h_{s(e)}U_eh_{t(e)}^{-1}$ and a face or loop holonomy is the ordered product of its edge variables.

[F2] [[def-qftx-wilson-loop]]: $W_\rho(C;U)=d^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(\rho(U_{e_1}\cdots U_{e_\ell}))$ for $d\geq1$.


## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $\ell=0$, both the loop holonomy and its conjugate are the identity. For $\ell\geq1$, write the successive vertices as $v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_\ell=v_0$. Substituting [F1] into the ordered product gives $U_C(h\cdot U)=(h_{v_0}U_{e_1}h_{v_1}^{-1})(h_{v_1}U_{e_2}h_{v_2}^{-1})\cdots(h_{v_{\ell-1}}U_{e_\ell}h_{v_0}^{-1})=h_{v_0}U_C(U)h_{v_0}^{-1}$, because each adjacent factor $h_{v_i}^{-1}h_{v_i}$ is the identity. The set-theoretic input is the inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ [A1]. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 Applying the homomorphism $\rho$ preserves conjugation, and trace is cyclic, so $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho(h_{v_0})\rho(U_C)\rho(h_{v_0})^{-1})=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho(U_C))$. Thus [F2] is gauge invariant; a cyclic rebase is the same trace after a cyclic permutation of factors. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Reversal replaces each edge matrix by its inverse in reverse order, hence replaces $\rho(U_C)$ by its inverse. Since $\rho(U_C)$ is unitary, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho(U_C)^{-1})=\overline{\operatorname{Tr}(\rho(U_C))}$; dividing by the real integer $d$ gives the stated complex-conjugation identity, including the empty-word case. [F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Use the matrix group $G_2=SU(2)=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_2,\ \det U=1\}$ with matrix multiplication and its standard real Lie-group structure. Its defining representation is $\rho_2(U)=U$ on $W=\mathbb C^2$ with Hermitian form $h(v,w)=v^*w$. In real coordinates every element has the form

$$
U(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x_0+ix_3&x_2+ix_1\\-x_2+ix_1&x_0-ix_3\end{pmatrix},\qquad x\in S^3:=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^3x_j^2=1\}.
$$

Let $\mu_2$ be the pushforward of normalized round surface measure on $S^3$ under $x\mapsto U(x)$. In spherical coordinates $x_0=\cos\theta$, $(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\sin\theta\,n$, $0\leq\theta\leq\pi$, $n\in S^2$, its coordinate density is $d\mu_2=(2/\pi)\sin^2\theta\,d\theta\,d\omega_2(n)$, where $n=(\sin\varphi\cos\psi,\sin\varphi\sin\psi,\cos\varphi)$ and $d\omega_2=(1/(4\pi))\sin\varphi\,d\varphi\,d\psi$ for $0\leq\varphi\leq\pi$, $0\leq\psi<2\pi$. Define the real class function $\tau(U):=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}_2(U)=x_0$.

For dimensionless $\beta\geq0$, define the pure-gauge Wilson plaquette action on any finite oriented lattice by

$$
S_\beta(U):=\beta\sum_{p}\bigl(1-\tau(U_p)\bigr),\qquad \beta=\frac{4}{g_0^2}
$$

when a dimensionless bare coupling $g_0>0$ is used. ## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M,N\geq1$ be integers and use the finite $M$-by-$N$ square lattice with free boundary (no periodic identifications and all boundary links retained), one $SU(2)$ link matrix per positively oriented edge, product normalized round measure, and only link variables (no matter variables), with the Wilson action $S_\beta(U)=\beta\sum_p(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}_2 U_p)$. Use the defining two-dimensional representation and normalized Wilson loop $W(C)=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}_2 U_C$, with edge matrices multiplied in traversal order. Let $\beta=4/g_0^2$ for dimensionless $g_0>0$, and restrict to the explicit strong-coupling window $0<\beta\leq1$ (equivalently $g_0^2\geq4$). For any axis-aligned rectangle contained in the lattice with corners $(a,c)$ and $(b,d)$, where $0\leq a<b\leq M$ and $0\leq c<d\leq N$, let $C_{a,b;c,d}$ be its boundary traversed counterclockwise from $(a,c)$. Its area in plaquette units is $A=(b-a)(d-c)$. The defining representation has nontrivial $\mathbb Z_2$ center charge because $-I_2$ acts as $-I_2$. Put

$$
\lambda(\beta):=\frac{\int_{SU(2)}\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}_2(U)e^{\beta\operatorname{Tr}_2(U)/2}\,d\mu_2(U)}{\int_{SU(2)}e^{\beta\operatorname{Tr}_2(U)/2}\,d\mu_2(U)},
$$

where $\mu_2$ is normalized round measure on $SU(2)\cong S^3$. Then $0<\lambda(\beta)<1$ and the exact finite-lattice expectation is

$$
\langle W(C_{a,b;c,d})\rangle_\beta=\lambda(\beta)^A=\exp\!\bigl(-\sigma_{\rm lat}(\beta)A\bigr),\qquad \sigma_{\rm lat}(\beta):=-\log\lambda(\beta)>0.
$$

The parameter $\beta$ and the lattice string tension $\sigma_{\rm lat}$ are dimensionless. The identity holds for every finite container and every stated rectangle; no infinite-area, infinite-volume, or continuum limit is taken, and no continuum confinement or mass-gap claim follows.

1.2 The coordinate map $\Xi:S^3\to SU(2)$, $x\mapsto U(x)$, is a bijection. Writing $a=x_0+ix_3$ and $b=x_2+ix_1$ recovers a unique $x\in S^3$, and direct multiplication shows every such $x$ gives an element of $SU(2)$. The map and its inverse are smooth coordinate maps. For round measure, use $x=q(\theta,\varphi,\psi)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta\sin\varphi\cos\psi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi\sin\psi,\sin\theta\cos\varphi)$ on $0<\theta,\varphi<\pi$, $0<\psi<2\pi$. Its three coordinate tangent vectors are pairwise orthogonal with squared lengths $1$, $\sin^2\theta$, and $\sin^2\theta\sin^2\varphi$, so the induced surface-area density is $\sin^2\theta\sin\varphi\,d\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi$. The chart boundary is a finite union of lower-dimensional smooth pieces and has zero three-dimensional surface area. Integration gives total area $(\int_0^\pi\sin^2\theta\,d\theta)(\int_0^\pi\sin\varphi\,d\varphi)(\int_0^{2\pi}d\psi)=2\pi^2$. Normalizing therefore gives $d\mu_2=(2/\pi)\sin^2\theta\,d\theta\,d\omega_2$ with $d\omega_2=(1/(4\pi))\sin\varphi\,d\varphi\,d\psi$, exactly the density stated in [F1], and total mass one. For $V\in SU(2)$, the maps $x\mapsto\Xi^{-1}(V\Xi(x))$ and $x\mapsto\Xi^{-1}(\Xi(x)V)$ are real-linear by [F6] and preserve $|x|$, since $\|\Xi(x)\|_F^2=2|x|^2$ and left and right multiplication by a unitary matrix preserve Frobenius norm. Their restrictions to $S^3$ are orthogonal transformations, which preserve round measure. Thus the pushforward formula [F1] makes $\mu_2$ a normalized bi-invariant Borel probability. [F1, F2, F4, F6, algebra]

2.1 In the coordinates established in step 1.2, $\tau(U)=\cos\theta$. Because $\mu_2$ is a probability and $-\beta\leq\beta\tau(U)\leq\beta$, the continuous factor $e^{\beta\tau}$ is bounded between $e^{-\beta}$ and $e^\beta$; hence $e^{-\beta}\leq I_0(\beta)\leq e^\beta$ and $I_0(\beta)$ is finite and positive. The density $z_\beta^{-1}e^{\beta\tau}$ therefore defines the probability $\nu_\beta$ [F5]. The angular vector $n\in S^2$ has mean zero by the measure-preserving symmetry $n\mapsto-n$. The coordinate integrands are continuous and bounded on the finite product-coordinate probability domain, so they are $L^1$ by [F5]; Fubini separates the angular and radial integrals. The matrix coordinates then give $\int Ue^{\beta\tau(U)}d\mu_2(U)=I_1(\beta)I_2$, proving $\int U\,d\nu_\beta(U)=\lambda(\beta)I_2$. [F1, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The transformation $U\mapsto-U$ corresponds to the orthogonal map $x\mapsto-x$, so it preserves $\mu_2$ and sends $\tau$ to $-\tau$. Consequently $I_1(\beta)=\int\tau(U)\sinh(\beta\tau(U))d\mu_2(U)>0$ for $\beta>0$: the integrand is nonnegative everywhere and strictly positive on, for example, the coordinate region $0<\theta<\pi/3$, which has positive measure by the density in step 1.2. Also $I_0-I_1=\int(1-\tau(U))e^{\beta\tau(U)}d\mu_2(U)>0$, since $\tau\leq1$ and equality holds only at the identity matrix, whose singleton has zero round measure by the coordinate density. Thus $0<\lambda<1$. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The measure from step 1.2 is invariant under every orthogonal transformation of $\mathbb R^4$. Coordinate sign changes give $\int x_0d\mu_2=0$ and permutation symmetry makes all four squared-coordinate integrals equal; integrating $\sum_{j=0}^3x_j^2=1$ therefore gives $\int x_0^2d\mu_2=1/4$. Taylor's formula for $e^{\beta x_0}$ has a remainder uniform for $|x_0|\leq1$ on a neighborhood of $\beta=0$; its integrals are finite because $\mu_2$ is a probability. Odd moments vanish under $x_0\mapsto-x_0$. Thus $I_0(\beta)=1+\beta^2/8+O(\beta^4)$ and $I_1(\beta)=\beta/4+O(\beta^3)$, so division gives $\lambda(\beta)=\beta/4+O(\beta^3)$. [F1, F5, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $F$ be a compact smooth manifold without boundary, possibly disconnected and nonorientable. Let $h$ be a unitary bundle automorphism covering the identity of $F$, obtained from the action of a fixed element of a compact torus, and acting on all symbol bundles compatibly with their maps. Put $n=\dim F$ componentwise. For a compact-support symbol class $a$ on $T^*F$, its trace-weighted compact-support Chern character is

$$\operatorname{ch}_{h,c}(a)=\sum_{\lambda}\lambda\,\operatorname{ch}_c(a_\lambda)\in H_c^{\mathrm{even}}(T^*F;\mathbb C),$$

where $a_\lambda$ is its symbol class on the $\lambda$-eigenbundles of $h$. The sum is finite on each compact disk-bundle representative; it is extended linearly to virtual classes. Here $\operatorname{ch}_c$ is the relative topological Chern character, not the Chern character of the alternating bundle restricted to the zero section.

Fix the following cotangent orientation and Bott normalization. If $\theta=\sum_j\xi_jdx_j$ is the tautological one-form, orient $T^*F$ by $(d\theta)^n/n!$, namely by $d\xi_1\wedge dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge d\xi_n\wedge dx_n$. The plane Bott class is the even-to-odd symbol $z:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ on the plane $z=x+i\xi$, with its relative-triple convention corresponding to $[\gamma]-1$ for the tautological Hopf line. Write $p_{F,!}:K_c^0(T^*F)\to\mathbb Z$ for the embedding construction: use this Bott Thom class on the doubled real normal bundle of an embedding $F\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^N$, extend by zero into $T^*\mathbb R^N$, and invert the same plane Bott external product on $T^*\mathbb R^N$. Its trace-weighted extension is $p_{F,!,h}(a)=\sum_\lambda\lambda p_{F,!}(a_\lambda)$. Then

$$p_{F,!,h}(a)=\int_{T^*F}\operatorname{ch}_{h,c}(a)\,\pi^*\operatorname{Td}(TF\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C).$$

For a degree-$2n$ compact-support cohomology class, the integral means its pairing with the relative fundamental class $[D_R(T^*F),S_R(T^*F)]$, using a radius $R$ containing its support in the disk interior, excision and the indicated orientation of the total space. Only the degree-$2n$ part is paired, and components are summed. This definition uses an orientation of the cotangent total space and requires no orientation of $F$.

The Todd class of a complex bundle with formal Chern roots $x_j$ means $\prod_j x_j/(1-e^{-x_j})$, expanded only through the dimension of the base. The integer construction is independent of the chosen embedding and tubular data.

In particular, let $M$ be a compact smooth torus manifold, $g$ a torus element, $F$ a component of $M^g$, $\nu$ its real normal bundle, and $i:T^*F\hookrightarrow T^*M$ the inclusion using an invariant metric. Put $e_g=\lambda_{-1}(\nu_{\mathbb C}^*)$ and let $\sigma\in K^0_{T,c}(T^*M)$ be any compact elliptic symbol class. The character of $e_g$ at $g$ is nonzero, and the trace-weighted Chern character extends to localization at virtual representations whose character at $g$ is nonzero. Whenever the representation-localized K-group supplies a class $b$ with $e_g b=i^*\sigma$ (in particular, the quotient $b=i^*\sigma/e_g$ furnished by K-localization), one has

$$p_{F,!,g}(b)=\int_{T^*F}\frac{\operatorname{ch}_{g,c}(i^*\sigma)}{\pi^*\operatorname{ch}_g(\lambda_{-1}(\nu_{\mathbb C}^*))}\,\pi^*\operatorname{Td}(TF_{\mathbb C}).$$

This is the characteristic-class comparison for a fixed component. It applies to the compact symbol of a general first-order elliptic complex after forming its even-to-odd elliptic symbol. It does not assert localization of equivariant K-theory or equality of analytic and topological indices; those are separate prerequisites for identifying the sum of these expressions with an analytic character. With the other common cotangent symplectic convention $-d\theta$, both displayed integrals acquire the factor $(-1)^n$.

[F1] The compact symbol and the exterior-algebra Bott symbol are the triples of [[def-equivariant-compact-symbol-k-theory]]. ## Proof

**Proof technique:** Compute the ordinary Thom Chern character on universal lines, descend by splitting, apply it to the doubled real normal of an embedding, and then take the trace on eigenbundles.

**Given:** The data in the Statement and the normalizations in [F1]–[F6].

1.1 A compact symbol on a vector bundle over a compact base can be restricted to a closed disk containing its noninvertibility set and radially identified with the disk/sphere pair. Radial contraction of the disk onto its zero section and [F7] identify both bundles there with pullbacks of bundles on the compact base. Its relative K-class is obtained by clutching its two bundles along the sphere using the boundary isomorphism. To see this in the based-quotient model, double the disk, glue the first bundle on its positive half to the second on its negative half, and subtract the doubled second bundle. Add a complement of the second bundle pulled back from the base, so the resulting bundle is trivialized on the negative disk; collapsing that disk gives a reduced virtual bundle on the Thom quotient. Such a complement exists: finitely many local frames and a subordinate partition of unity embed a bundle in a finite trivial bundle, and its orthogonal complement supplies it. Different complements have a common stabilization, and changing the radius or boundary collar gives a homotopy. Conversely, pull a reduced bundle on the quotient back to the positive disk with its boundary trivialization. These operations are inverse after adding elementary triples: the negative half is precisely the trivialized summand removed in the collapse. Thus the ordinary compact triple character used here is [F2]'s relative character, and it respects pullback, extension by zero and products. For products the clutching construction gives tensor products of the resulting reduced virtual bundles; hence [F2]'s ring identity gives the relative product identity. [F1, F2, F6, F7, construct]

1.2 On $\Lambda^\bullet\mathbb C^r$ put $c(v)=\varepsilon_v-\varepsilon_v^*$ for real $v\in\mathbb C^r$. These are skew-adjoint Clifford matrices; for a unitary basis their two-dimensional factors are exactly the matrices in [F3]'s supplier, and their graded tensors span the full matrix algebra. The action $\Lambda^\bullet u$ of $u\in U(r)$ preserves grading and conjugates $c(v)$ to $c(uv)$. Choose either spin lift $s$ of the realification of $u$. The operator $(\Lambda^\bullet u)\rho(s)^{-1}$ commutes with every Clifford matrix, hence is a unit scalar $z$. Replacing $s$ by $-s$ replaces $z$ by $-z$, so $u\mapsto[s,z]\in\operatorname{Spin}^c(2r)$ is well-defined; local continuous lifts to the spin double cover show continuity, and multiplication of the implementing matrices proves it is a homomorphism. Thus the unitary frame bundle of $W$ induces a specified Spin-c lift whose associated spinor bundle is $\Lambda^\bullet W$. Its Clifford symbol is isomorphic as a relative triple to $D=\varepsilon_v+\varepsilon_v^*$: multiply degree $2j$ in the source by $(-1)^j$ and degree $2j+1$ in the target by $(-1)^j$; exterior multiplication is unchanged and contraction changes sign. In rank zero use the trivial lift and the even line. Therefore [F3] applies to the exact exterior symbol in [F1], with its plane map $z$ and its direct-sum product. [F1, F3, construct, algebra]

1.3 Choose a smooth embedding $f:F\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^N$ and its normal bundle $V$. Such an embedding can be constructed from finitely many coordinate charts and bump functions: take the vector of all functions $\phi_\alpha$ and $\phi_\alpha x_{\alpha,j}$, where the $\phi_\alpha$ are supported inside charts and their positive sets cover $F$. Equality of these vectors determines a common chart with $\phi_\alpha>0$ and then its coordinates, giving injectivity; differentiating the same coordinates shows injectivity of the derivative. Compactness makes it an embedding. An ambient metric splits $f^*T\mathbb R^N=TF\oplus V$ and embeds $T^*F$ into $T^*\mathbb R^N$ by zero normal covector. Its normal bundle, pulled back to $T^*F$, is $V\oplus V^*$: a connection splits horizontal and vertical tangent directions, and the two missing directions are the normal base vector and normal covector. Homotopies of the connection preserve this identification. At the zero section the cotangent symplectic form is the direct sum of the forms on $TF\oplus T^*F$ and $V\oplus V^*$; their symplectic orientations therefore multiply. Fiber dilation contracts $T^*F$ onto its zero section and preserves nondegeneracy, so the same orientation identity holds everywhere. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let $L$ be a complex line, $x=c_1(L)$, $u_L$ its complex-oriented cohomological Thom class, and $\tau_L$ the plane-normalized Bott symbol [F3]. Thom isomorphism uniquely writes $\operatorname{ch}_c(\tau_L)=u_L A(L)$. The zero-section identity gives $x A(L)=1-e^x$. This equation alone cannot be divided by $x$ on an arbitrary base. Instead apply it to the tautological line on $\mathbb{CP}^k$: for each coefficient through degree $2k-2$, multiplication by $x$ is injective by [F4], so $A(\gamma)=(1-e^x)/x$ through that degree. For any prescribed finite degree choose the stage one degree higher. Compatibility under stage restriction determines every required coefficient, including the constant $-1$. A line on a finite CW base is pulled back from a sufficiently large finite stage of its classifying map, so naturality proves
$$\operatorname{ch}_c(\tau_L)=-u_L e^x\operatorname{Td}(L)^{-1}.$$
This also verifies the sign: on a complex-oriented plane the compact character of the prescribed Bott generator integrates to $-1$. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For a rank-$r$ complex bundle $W$, pull to its flag splitting space. There $W=\bigoplus_jL_j$, and [F3], [F5] and the product identity in step 1.1 give
$$\operatorname{ch}_c(\tau_W)=(-1)^r u_W e^{c_1(W)}\operatorname{Td}(W)^{-1}.$$
Indeed multiplication of the line formulas gives the displayed factor, the sum of the line first Chern classes is $c_1(W)$, and the product of their Todd factors defines the Todd class. To descend, first write the left-hand side as $u_W A(W)$ by the ordinary Thom isomorphism. Pullback preserves $u_W$, and [F4]'s rational injectivity identifies the unique coefficient $A(W)$ with the displayed symmetric series. This proves the formula on the base, including rank zero. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $V$ be a real rank-$r$ metric bundle and identify its double $V\oplus V^*$ with $V_{\mathbb C}$ by $(v,\eta)\mapsto v+i\eta^\sharp$. The real structure identifies $V_{\mathbb C}$ with its complex conjugate. Consequently $2c_1(V_{\mathbb C})=0$ and $c_1(V_{\mathbb C})=0$ rationally. The complex orientation is $dv_1\wedge d\eta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dv_r\wedge d\eta_r$, while the cotangent normal orientation is $d\eta_1\wedge dv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge d\eta_r\wedge dv_r$; their ratio is $(-1)^r$. If $u_-$ denotes the latter Thom class, step 3.1 therefore becomes
$$\operatorname{ch}_c(\tau_{V_{\mathbb C}})=u_-\operatorname{Td}(V_{\mathbb C})^{-1}.$$
All formulas are invariant under real orthogonal frame changes: their doubled real determinant is positive. Thus they apply without an orientation on $V$ or on its base. [F1, F5, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Form $j_!(a)$ by pulling $a$ to that normal bundle, multiplying by $\tau_{V_{\mathbb C}}$, and extending from a tubular neighborhood by zero. A tubular neighborhood exists here directly from the ambient Euclidean normal map: its derivative at the zero section is invertible; the inverse function theorem and compactness of the part of the zero section meeting the support give an injective sufficiently small neighborhood. Shrinking that neighborhood changes its collapse by a radial homotopy. Step 1.1 and step 4.1 give
$$\operatorname{ch}_c(j_!a)=j_*\bigl(\operatorname{ch}_c(a)\,\pi^*\operatorname{Td}(V_{\mathbb C})^{-1}\bigr),$$
where $j_*$ means multiplication by $u_-$ and extension by zero in ordinary compact-support cohomology. For the pairing in [F8], $\int j_*\alpha=\int\alpha$: subdivide a relative fundamental cycle subordinate to normal trivializing neighborhoods, and apply the relative cup-cap pairing on each product disk. The ordered normal Thom generator evaluates to $1$ on its normal disk by normalization, leaving the corresponding tangent coefficient; summing these coefficients gives the original pairing. The local generators of the total fundamental class are exactly these ordered products by step 1.3. Thus this is a cohomological fundamental-class pairing and requires no implicit de Rham comparison. This argument also works for virtual classes and for nonorientable $F$, since its cotangent orientation is global. [F2, F5, F8, step 1.1, step 1.3, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 By [F3], $K_c^0(T^*\mathbb R^N)$ is the infinite cyclic group generated by the $N$-fold plane Bott product, whose character integrates to $1$ with the $d\theta$ orientation: each factor has complex-oriented integral $-1$ by step 2.1, and reversing each of the $N$ plane orientations supplies another $(-1)^N$. Thus the integer coefficient of $j_!a$ in this generator is its integrated compact character. Since $TF_{\mathbb C}\oplus V_{\mathbb C}$ is trivial, multiplicativity of the Todd series gives $\operatorname{Td}(V_{\mathbb C})^{-1}=\operatorname{Td}(TF_{\mathbb C})$. Integrating step 5.1 proves the first formula for the ordinary class $a$. Its right-hand side uses no embedding or tubular data, so the integer defined by any such construction is independent of those choices. [F3, step 2.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Put $H=\overline{\langle h\rangle}$ in the acting torus. Since $h$ fixes every point of $F$, continuity makes $H$ act trivially on $F$, hence on $T^*F$. On a compact disk-bundle representative each bundle has only finitely many $H$-weights. Here is a local justification of the finiteness assertion: in a unitary local frame the character is a continuous function of the base point, uniformly on the compact group $H$; its Fourier coefficients are the integer multiplicities of characters. Close base points have uniformly close characters and hence all multiplicities equal, because the coefficient differences have absolute value less than $1$. The weight list is locally constant and the disk has finitely many components. The weight projections are the integrals of the action against the conjugate characters, so are continuous projections of locally constant rank and define eigenbundles. Every equivariant symbol map preserves them. Direct sums, homotopies and elementary triples preserve the resulting weighted ordinary K-class, so $\operatorname{ch}_{h,c}$ is well-defined. Tensoring eigenbundles multiplies eigenvalues, and [F2] gives multiplicativity with an absolute bundle class. Weightwise application of step 6.1 proves the trace-weighted formula. Its degree-zero value on a bundle over a point is $\operatorname{tr}(h)$, whereas the ordinary Chern character's degree-zero value is its dimension; thus a degree-zero Borel rank cannot replace this operation. [F1, F2, step 6.1, construct, algebra]

8.1 On $F\subset M^g$, the fixed subspace of $dg$ is $TF$; the invariant metric gives an orthogonal splitting $TM|_F=TF\oplus\nu$ and no $1$-eigenvector in $\nu$. The exterior-power identity in [F1] gives the degree-zero term
$$\operatorname{ch}_g(e_g)_{[0]}=\det_{\mathbb C}(I-g|_{\nu_{\mathbb C}^*})=\det_{\mathbb R}(I-g|_\nu)>0.$$
In the finite-dimensional cohomology ring of $F$, all positive-degree classes are nilpotent. Writing $\operatorname{ch}_g(e_g)=c+u$ with $c$ the nonzero locally constant term, its inverse is the finite geometric sum $c^{-1}\sum_{k\ge0}(-u/c)^k$. Similarly a representation $s$ of nonzero character acts under step 7.1 as the invertible scalar $\chi_s(g)$, so both the weighted character and the weighted pushforward extend by division by this scalar to representation localization. For a localized K-class $b$ with $e_g b=i^*\sigma$, multiplicativity forces $\operatorname{ch}_{g,c}(b)=\operatorname{ch}_{g,c}(i^*\sigma)/\operatorname{ch}_g(e_g)$. Substitution in step 7.1 proves the second displayed formula whenever the localized quotient exists. In particular it applies to the quotient furnished by a separately proved K-localization theorem; no such theorem was used to prove this comparison. [F1, F2, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 For an elliptic complex, let $s$ be its symbol differential at a nonzero real covector. Exactness implies that $s+s^*$ has zero kernel: its square is $ss^*+s^*s$, whose quadratic form is $\|su\|^2+\|s^*u\|^2$, and an element killed by both is an element of $\ker s$ orthogonal to $\operatorname{im}s=\ker s$. Thus its even-to-odd block is invertible and defines the same compact-support construction, with no Dirac or isolated-point restriction. A zero-dimensional $F$ has $T^*F=F$, positive point orientations and Todd class $1$, so the integral is the finite fiber trace sum. Finally $(-d\theta)^n=(-1)^n(d\theta)^n$, proving the stated change-of-convention factor. These observations include the empty manifold, zero symbols and rank-zero normals. AC has been used only through the listed topological suppliers and finite smooth bundle constructions. [A1, F1, step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The ordinary Thom comparison and the trace weighting are proved here. To obtain an equivariant analytic fixed-component index theorem one still needs (i) an equivariant compact-support K-localization theorem giving the normal inverse and compatibility of the topological pushforward, and (ii) equality of the equivariant analytic index with that pushforward for general elliptic symbols. The ordinary Spin-c Thom theorem and a Dirac index formula alone do not prove (ii).

Gilkey uses $dx_1\wedge d\xi_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_n\wedge d\xi_n$ as the cotangent symplectic orientation in §4.4; the accompanying dimension sign is essential when converting to that convention. Heitsch's Theorem 2.1 displays $(-1)^n$ in its ordinary symbol formula. These source comparisons fix conventions; they are not premises replacing the Thom computation above.

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $T=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r$, $r\ge0$, act smoothly by isometries on a compact smooth manifold $M$ without boundary. Let $E^0,\ldots,E^N$ be smooth finite-rank Hermitian complex bundles and $d_j:C^\infty(M,E^j)\to C^\infty(M,E^{j+1})$ first-order differential maps with $d_{j+1}d_j=0$, setting $d_{-1}=d_N=0$. Their positive-frequency symbols use $\partial_x^\alpha\mapsto(i\xi)^\alpha$. Assume the symbol sequence is exact for every nonzero real cotangent vector. A jointly smooth unitary bundle action has maps $\rho_t^j(x):E_x^j\to E_{t\cdot x}^j$, with $\rho_e^j(x)=I$ and $\rho_{st}^j(x)=\rho_s^j(t\cdot x)\rho_t^j(x)$; set $(U_t^js)(x)=\rho_t^j(t^{-1}\cdot x)s(t^{-1}\cdot x)$ and require $U_t^{j+1}d_j=d_jU_t^j$.

Write $d=\bigoplus_jd_j$, let $d^*$ be its formal adjoint for the invariant metrics and Riemannian volume, and put $D=d+d^*$. Its even-to-odd symbol defines the compact-support class $\sigma\in K^0_{T,c}(T^*M)$. The cohomology groups $H^j=\ker d_j/\operatorname{im}d_{j-1}$ are finite dimensional. Define $\operatorname{Ind}_T(E^\bullet)=\sum_j(-1)^j[H^j]\in R(T)$, where $R(T)$ is the Grothendieck ring of finite-dimensional continuous complex representations.

For any $g\in T$, write $M^g=\coprod_aF_a$ for its finitely many connected fixed components, $\nu_a=(TF_a)^\perp\subset TM|_{F_a}$, $\pi_a:T^*F_a\to F_a$, and $i_a:T^*F_a\hookrightarrow T^*M$ for extension of covectors by zero on $\nu_a$. Put $\nu_{a,\mathbb C}=\nu_a\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ and $e_a=\lambda_{-1}(\nu_{a,\mathbb C}^*)=\sum_k(-1)^k[\Lambda^k\nu_{a,\mathbb C}^*]$. Then

$$\chi_{\operatorname{Ind}_T(E^\bullet)}(g)=\sum_a\int_{T^*F_a}\frac{\operatorname{ch}_{g,c}(i_a^*\sigma)}{\pi_a^*\operatorname{ch}_g(e_a)}\,\pi_a^*\operatorname{Td}(TF_a\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C).$$

For a symbol on the $g$-fixed base, $\operatorname{ch}_{g,c}$ means the compact-support relative Chern character weighted by the eigenvalue of $g$ on each eigenbundle; for an absolute virtual bundle $V$, $\operatorname{ch}_g(V)=\sum_\lambda\lambda\operatorname{ch}(V_\lambda)$. The Todd class is $\prod_jx_j/(1-e^{-x_j})$ in formal Chern roots, truncated in each degree. The integral is the oriented compact-support cohomological pairing on the cotangent bundle, oriented by $d\theta=\sum_jd\xi_j\wedge dx_j$. The denominator has nonzero degree-zero term $\det_{\mathbb R}(I-dg|_{\nu_a})$, so its positive-degree part is inverted by a finite nilpotent series. Its full characteristic class is retained for a positive-dimensional component. The degree-zero value of $\operatorname{ch}_g$ is the trace at $g$; it is distinct from the degree-zero rank of a Borel equivariant Chern character.

At an element where the fixed locus changes, the formula uses that element's actual fixed components and normal bundles. It applies also at $g=e$, when $F=M$ and the normal denominator is $1$; it asserts no transversally elliptic distribution formula. If the fixed components are isolated points, it specializes to

$$\chi_{\operatorname{Ind}_T(E^\bullet)}(g)=\sum_{x\in M^g}\frac{\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g^j(x)|_{E_x^j})}{|\det_{\mathbb R}(I-dg_x)|}.$$

Thus the earlier spectral isolated-point case retains its weaker choice assumption.

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $G$ be a compact Lie group and $X$ a compact smooth $G$-manifold without boundary. A compact-support symbol triple on $T^*X$ consists of finite-rank continuous complex $G$-vector bundles $A,B$ and a continuous equivariant bundle map $b:A\to B$ which is an isomorphism off a compact subset. Triples are compared by equivariant bundle isomorphisms, block sum, continuous homotopies with a common compact support, and addition or removal of elementary triples whose map is everywhere invertible. These conventions concern actual bundle maps and their deformations; no previously defined equivariant $K$-group is assumed.

Every such triple has an index $a_G(A,B,b)\in R(G)$, where $R(G)$ is the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional continuous complex $G$-representations. It is realized as $[\ker P]-[\ker P^*]$ by a $G$-invariant elliptic order-zero operator on smooth bundles over $X$. Its symbol is obtained by smoothing the triple, identifying its bundles with pullbacks from the zero section by radial transport, and replacing the invertible exterior symbol by a homogeneous symbol. The index is independent of these operations, respects all the comparisons above and is additive under block sum. For a homogeneous elliptic symbol of any integer order, it equals the Fredholm index of every invariant classical or simultaneous-Sobolev-closure realization with that symbol.

The construction is natural under equivariant diffeomorphisms and restriction along homomorphisms between compact Lie groups. Tensoring all data by a finite-dimensional representation tensors the index by that representation. On a point it is the difference of the two fiber representations. Let $0\to C^\infty(X,E^0)\xrightarrow{d_0}\cdots\xrightarrow{d_{N-1}}C^\infty(X,E^N)\to0$ be a finite first-order differential complex, so $d_{j+1}d_j=0$, whose positive-frequency principal-symbol sequence is exact at every nonzero real cotangent vector. For a $G$-action by chain maps with section action $U_gu(x)=\rho_g(g^{-1}x)u(g^{-1}x)$, put $H^j=\ker d_j/\operatorname{im}d_{j-1}$, with $d_{-1}=d_N=0$. Its symbol index is $\sum_j(-1)^j[H^j]$; these cohomology representations are finite dimensional and have unique harmonic representatives. This includes the de Rham complex.

Here is the controlled noncompact form. Let $U$ have an open equivariant embedding into a compact closed smooth $G$-manifold. For a compact-support triple on $T^*U$, its index can be computed after replacing it, through the same comparisons on a neighborhood of its support, by smooth base-bundle data $E,F$ and a homogeneous degree-zero symbol $c:\pi^*E\to\pi^*F$ for which $E=F=U\times V$ and $c=I_V$ outside a compact invariant subset of $U$, with $V$ a finite-dimensional representation. There is an elliptic invariant realization equal to the exterior bundle isomorphism off one compact invariant $L\subset U$, in both the source and target kernel variables; explicitly it has the form $P=\eta_2P_0\eta_1+h(1-\eta_1)$ with nested compactly supported cutoffs and exterior isomorphism $h$. Extending the bundles and this operator to any compact equivariant ambient manifold by the exterior trivializations gives the same virtual kernel representation. Thus the index is independent of that ambient embedding and satisfies excision for open equivariant inclusions whenever such compact ambients are supplied. No compactification of an arbitrary $G$-manifold is asserted.

$$B_1A_0=A_1B_0,\qquad B_0^*A_1^*=A_0^*B_1^*,\qquad B_1^*A_1=A_0B_0^*,\qquad B_0A_0^*=A_1^*B_1.$$

The adjoints are with respect to the invariant product density on $Y$ obtained from the base density and the $H$-invariant fiber density. Define

$$D=\begin{pmatrix}A_0&-B_1^*\\ B_0&A_1^*\end{pmatrix}:\mathcal E^{00}\oplus\mathcal E^{11}\longrightarrow\mathcal E^{10}\oplus\mathcal E^{01}.$$

Then $D:H^1\to L^2$ is Fredholm, both its kernel and its adjoint kernel are finite-dimensional smooth $T$-representations, and its principal symbol represents the graded product of $a$ and $b$. Explicitly, a connection splitting of a covector on $Y$ into horizontal $\xi$ and vertical $\eta$ gives the product symbol

$$d_{\mathrm{prod}}(y;\xi,\eta)=\begin{pmatrix}a(p_Yy,\xi)\otimes I&-I\otimes b(f,\eta)^*\\ I\otimes b(f,\eta)&a(p_Yy,\xi)^*\otimes I\end{pmatrix}.$$

This matrix is interpreted using an associated-bundle trivialization; its homotopy class is independent of the connection. The actual glued lift symbol need only be homotopic through invertible joint symbols to this matrix.

Let $K=\ker B$ and $L=\ker B^*$, with their finite-dimensional $H\times T$ actions, and put $K_P=P\times_H K$, $L_P=P\times_H L$. The restricted lifts give elliptic operators $C_K:E^0\otimes K_P\to E^1\otimes K_P$ and $C_L$ with $K$ replaced by $L$, whose symbols are $a\otimes I$. For $\operatorname{Ind}_T Q=[\ker Q]-[\ker Q^*]\in R(T)$, where $R(T)$ is the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional continuous complex $T$-representations, one has

$$\operatorname{Ind}_T D=\operatorname{Ind}_T C_K-\operatorname{Ind}_T C_L.$$

Thus the analytic symbol index of the associated product is the base symbol index twisted by the associated virtual vertical index $K_P-L_P$. For a product bundle with independent commuting group actions this specializes to multiplication of representation-valued indices. The same external-product identity holds for compactly supported elliptic symbol data on invariant open manifolds when their indices are defined by the controlled compactification and excision construction.
